name: Alien Gambit & Martian Gambit
family: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Caro-Kann Main Line (knight sacrifices on f7 and e6)
summary: Two modern knight sacrifices against the Caro-Kann main line, created by Bulgarian CM Volen Dyulgerov (Witty_Alien) and popularised in 2024 by GothamChess and Eric Rosen. After 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 (3.Nd2 dxe4 4.Nxe4 transposes), the Alien Gambit answers 4...Nf6 with 5.Ng5 h6 6.Nxf7!? Kxf7 7.Nf3, and the Martian Gambit answers 4...Bf5 with 5.Ng5 Bg6 6.N1f3 h6 7.Ne6!? fxe6 8.Ne5. Be honest with yourself: both sacrifices are objectively unsound (about -2.7 after 7...c5! in the Alien, about -1.5 after 8...Bf5! in the Martian), but Black has to find narrow defences while his king is exposed, and in practice White scores very well (around 64% for the Martian on Lichess). When Black finds the refutation, keep pieces on the board, castle, bring every piece toward the king and look for checks, forks and pins on e6 and f7. If Black declines with 5...e6, 5...c5 or 5...Bf5 (Alien) or never plays ...h6 (Martian), we switch to normal, healthy Caro-Kann play.
keyIdeas: The sacrifice only works after ...h6: the Alien needs 4...Nf6 5.Ng5 h6, the Martian needs 4...Bf5 5.Ng5 Bg6 6.N1f3 h6. Without ...h6, play normal moves.
Alien follow-up: Nf3, Ne5+, Bc4+ or Bd3, Qe2 and often O-O-O with h4-g4-g5. The black king on f7 or g8 sits on the a2-g8 diagonal and in reach of Ne5+ forks.
Martian follow-up: 8.Ne5 hits the g6-bishop. Against 8...Bf7?! play 9.Bc4 and attack e6; against 8...Bf5! play 9.g4; against 8...Bh7 play 9.Bc4.
Pins on the a2-g8 / c4-f7 diagonal decide many games: ...Qd5 or ...Qxd5 with the king on f7 loses the queen to Bc4, and ...Bh7 with the king on g8 can allow Bxe6#.
Knight forks: Ne5+ hits f7 together with d7, g4, c4 and c6. A black bishop on g4 or a queen on c4 is often lost to it.
Ng6 harasses a rook still on h8 (the king on g8 blocks it in), often winning back the exchange.
Objectively both gambits lose against best play, so the goal is practical: create problems, keep the initiative and avoid trading queens.
typicalPlans: Alien vs 7...c5: Bc4+, Qe2, Bd2, O-O-O, h4, Rhe1 and g4-g5, piling up on e6 and opening files near the king.
Alien vs quiet development (...e6, ...Nbd7): Bd3, O-O, Qe2, Nh4 and f4-f5 to open the f-file.
Martian vs 8...Bf7: Bc4, Qd3 or Qe2, f4-f5 and O-O; watch for Nxf7 followed by Qg4 and Bxe6+ if g4 is left uncovered.
Martian vs 8...Bf5 or 8...Bh7: g4, Bc4, Bf4, O-O and tactical knight jumps such as Ng6 with discovered attacks.
Against the declines: trade the light-squared bishops (Bd3 or Bb5+), develop with Ne2 or Nf3 and O-O, and play a normal equal Caro-Kann.
commonMistakes: Sacrificing when Black has not played ...h6: without that move the knight on f7 or e6 achieves nothing.
Expecting the gambits to be sound: after 7...c5! (Alien) or 8...Bf5! (Martian) Black is better, so do not panic or try to force mate. Keep developing and keep making threats.
Trading queens early: without queens Black's extra piece usually wins the endgame.
Playing the tempting 8.g4?! in the 5...h6 6.Nxf7 Martian line: 8...Nxg4! wins another pawn. Check first with Ne5+.
Answering 5...e6 6.N1f3 h6 with 7.g4?: 7...hxg5 just wins the knight. Retreat with 7.Nh3, or prefer 6.Bd3 h6 7.N5f3.
Grabbing back material too soon: in the Martian, 9...Nd7? is punished by 10.Nxf7! and 11.Qg4, not by 10.Bxe6? Nxe5.
As Black (what to expect from opponents): 8...Bf7?! in the Martian, 7...Bg4? and 7...Qd5? in the Alien, and 5...Ngf6?? after 4...Nd7 5.Qe2 are the classic blunders.

lines.name: Alien Gambit: Accepted, 7...c5 refutation (main line)
lines.description: The critical test of the Alien Gambit and the line you must know. After 7...c5! Black returns to the centre before our attack starts; we answer with Bc4+, Qe2, Bd2 and O-O-O, then storm with h4-g4-g5 and pile up on e6.
lines.evaluation: Black is objectively better (about -2.8), but his king is stuck on f7 and every white piece joins the attack: excellent practical chances, especially in faster games.

moves.why: Starts the Caro-Kann fight: Black's ...c6 and ...d5 aim for a solid pawn chain, so we take the centre first and fight for d5 and e5.
The Caro-Kann: ...c6 supports ...d5 and lets the c8-bishop come out before ...e6 closes it in, unlike the French.
Builds the big centre with e4 and d4; Black must now challenge e4 with ...d5 rather than simply develop.
The Caro-Kann idea: ...d5 attacks e4, and if we exchange, ...cxd5 recaptures and keeps the pawn chain intact.
Defends e4 with a piece so that after ...dxe4 we recapture with the knight and keep the centre; 3.Nd2 transposes after ...dxe4 4.Nxe4.
The main Caro-Kann line: Black gives up the e4 pawn and opens the d-file and the c8-bishop, aiming for ...Bf5 or ...Nd7.
Recaptures and centralises the knight on e4, where it eyes f6, g5 and d6: the squares the Alien and Martian sacrifices use.
Challenges the e4-knight at once. Most players expect 5.Nxf6+, and that is where the Alien Gambit springs its surprise.
Avoids the knight trade and stares at f7, the weakest point in Black's camp. Now the natural 5...h6, kicking the knight, walks into the Alien Gambit.
Natural: Black attacks the knight and expects it to retreat to e4, f3 or h3. This is the move the Alien Gambit is waiting for.

The Alien Gambit! A deliberate knight sacrifice: we give a whole piece for one pawn to drag the king to f7 and open the f-file and the a2-g8 diagonal. Objectively unsound (the engine says about -2.5), but Black must find several accurate moves to prove it.
Practically forced: if Black leaves the knight alone it takes on h8 or d8 (6...Qc7?! 7.Nxh8 or 6...Bg4? 7.Qxg4 and White is winning). Now the king sits on f7, open to checks.
The main move: develops calmly and prepares Ne5+ (forking the king with anything on d7, g4 or c6) and Bc4+ along the light squares. Our attack is built from Ne5+, Bc4+ or Bd3, Qe2 and sometimes g4.
The engine's refutation (about -2.7 for Black). Black hits d4 at once, freeing the queen and c8-bishop and opening lines before our attack is ready.

The most testing reply: the check forces Black to block. 8...Nd5 meets 9.Ne5+ Kg8 10.Qh5 with a dangerous attack, and 8...Be6?? 9.Ne5+ just wins for White, so Black plays ...e6 and locks in his own bishop.
Best: blocks the check and covers d5 and f5, but it shuts in the c8-bishop and leaves e6 as a target on the e-file.

Puts the queen on the e-file against e6 and clears the way for Bd2 and O-O-O. We are not trying to win the piece back at once; we want every piece in the attack first. (9.Ne5+ Kg8 10.Ng6 is a sharp alternative.)
Black takes the d4-pawn. Material is now a clean knight up for Black (he has two knights to our one, bishops 2 v 2, and the pawns are level at six each), so every White move must build the attack.
Clears the back rank for O-O-O and takes the sting out of ...Bb4+. The d4-pawn can wait; Black's king is the real target.
Develops and protects d4. Black's plan is ...Nd5, ...Qd6 or ...Bd6 and eventually ...Kg8 to untangle.
Castles long so the rooks join at once: Rhe1 piles up on e6 and the kingside pawns are free to storm with h4 and g4-g5.
The best defensive post: the knight blocks our c4-bishop's diagonal toward e6 and the king, and can jump to b4 or f4.
Starts the pawn storm: g4-g5 will hit the h6-pawn and open files near the black king, and the rook can swing over via h3. An extra piece means little if the king gets caught.
Covers e6 a second time and eyes the long diagonal toward g3. Black wants ...Bd7, ...Be7 and ...Kg8 to connect his rooks.
Every white piece is now in play and the e6-pawn is under fire. Next come g4-g5 and tactics on e6, such as Bxd5 exd5 opening the e-file, or Ne5+ at the right moment.
Black finishes developing and prepares ...Be7 and ...Rhf8 or ...Kg8. Once his rooks connect the extra piece should tell, so keep the pressure on.

A useful safety move: the king leaves the c-file before Black's rooks arrive. Plan from here: g4-g5 to break open the h6-pawn and the g-file, Ne5+ when it gains time, and Bxd5 exd5 when that opens the e-file. Objectively Black is better, but one inaccuracy can lose on the spot.

lines.name: Alien Gambit: 7...c5 8.d5!? trap (8...Qxd5?? 9.Bc4!)
lines.description: After 7...c5 the cheeky 8.d5 offers a pawn so that ...Qxd5 puts the black queen on the same diagonal as the king on f7. It is a trap, not a good move: 8.Bc4+ is objectively better, and if Black declines with 8...Kg8 or 8...Qd6 we are about one pawn worse off than after 8.Bc4+.
lines.evaluation: After the trap (8...Qxd5?? 9.Bc4!) White is winning, about +6. If Black declines the pawn, Black is clearly better, about -3.6 to -3.8.

lines.name: Alien Gambit: Accepted, 7...Bf5 8.Ne5+ Kg8 9.Bc4+ e6 10.g4
lines.description: A popular club reply. After 8.Ne5+ Kg8 9.Bc4+ e6?! 10.g4! Black's bishop runs out of squares and the position is roughly equal; the more accurate 9...Nd5! (10.Qf3 Be6 11.O-O and Ng6 to hit h8) keeps Black better.
lines.evaluation: About equal after 10.g4 (engine -0.1 to -0.4); Black must find 10...Be4 or 10...b5.

lines.description: The most natural retreat of the f5-bishop takes away the king's last flight square. A pattern worth remembering: king on g8, rook on h8, bishop on f8, and a bishop check on the a2-g8 diagonal.
